stem: A nurse is preparing to dispose of suctioned body fluids from a full suction canister. Which action is appropriate?

options.A: Follow the facility regulated-medical-waste plan and applicable state/local requirements; sanitary-sewer disposal may be used when those requirements permit it
options.B: Always place the entire filled canister in regular trash because suctioned fluids are not regulated medical waste
options.C: Always pour suctioned fluids into any available sink regardless of local sewer-discharge rules
options.D: Always place every suction canister in a sharps container even when no sharps are present

rationale: CDC guidance states that bulk blood and bloody body-fluid specimens are major categories requiring special handling and that federal, state, and local requirements determine regulated-medical-waste practices. CDC also states that sanitary sewers may be used for blood and suctioned fluids when local sewage-discharge requirements are met and the state accepts that disposal method. Therefore the nurse should follow the facility's approved waste plan and applicable jurisdictional rules rather than assume one disposal route is universal. A is the best answer.
educational_objective: Manage suctioned body-fluid waste according to the facility's regulated-medical-waste plan and applicable state/local requirements, recognizing that sanitary-sewer disposal is acceptable only where permitted.
source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
source_document_title: Guidelines for Environmental Infection Control in Health-Care Facilities — Regulated Medical Waste
source_version_date: CDC web guidance updated 2024-01-08; recommendations page updated 2024-04-12; accessed 2026-08-17
source_locator: Regulated Medical Waste §1 Epidemiology/Categories: bulk blood and bloody body-fluid specimens require special handling and federal/state/local rules define regulated waste; §5 Discharging Blood, Fluids to Sanitary Sewers or Septic Tanks and Summary Recommendation I.IV.E: sanitary sewers may be used for blood and suctioned fluids when local discharge requirements are met and the state permits it
source_claim_supported: Suctioned body fluids do not have one universal disposal route; disposal must follow the approved waste plan and applicable jurisdictional requirements, with sanitary-sewer disposal permitted in jurisdictions that allow it.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — Handling Hazardous and Infectious Materials, printed p.25 / PDF p.29: identify biohazardous and infectious materials; follow procedures for handling biohazardous and hazardous materials
blueprint_topic: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — body-fluid/regulated medical waste handling
correction_summary: Removed the false universal rule that every full suction canister must be discarded as biohazardous waste. Replaced it with CDC's jurisdiction-dependent disposal rule and the requirement to follow the facility regulated-medical-waste plan.
audit_findings: A accurately preserves CDC's state/local/facility dependency and sewer-disposal option. B incorrectly classifies all suctioned fluid as ordinary waste. C ignores jurisdictional discharge restrictions and appropriate disposal procedures. D misuses a sharps container for a non-sharps waste stream. The revised item avoids inventing a universal volume threshold or container route. NCSBN 2026 mapping is explicit; independent second pass found one best answer.
audit_reviewer: GPT-5.6 Sol Rule 1 — item-by-item semantic audit
final_reaudit_scope: current CDC regulated-medical-waste guidance; exact locator; claim-by-claim; A-D distractor audit; ambiguity/second-answer/cueing; NCSBN 2026 blueprint; independent adversarial second pass
